content: The rollout of the Xpert MTB/RIF diagnostic tool for tuberculosis (TB) in South Africa was evaluated for its cost-effectiveness through a real-world cost analysis and economic evaluation. This study, published in The Lancet Global Health in 2017, aimed to provide insights into the financial implications of implementing this diagnostic intervention. To design a representative sampling frame for TB costing studies, it is essential to synthesize available country-level data on TB services. This helps outline the sampling frame from which eventual site selection is made. However, logistical challenges and budget constraints often limit cost estimates in lowand middle-income countries to a small number of sites (fewer than 10). Larger studies, particularly in the context of HIV, have emerged in recent years, revealing significant cost variations. This suggests that relying on small sample sizes may yield unrepresentative results. Even with limited site selection, explicit consideration and transparency in the sampling frame and selection methods can help others apply cost estimates to different settings. The structure of the health system in a given setting determines where interventions of interest occur. For example, TB symptom screening might take place in clinics, while microscopy tests are conducted in laboratories. Developing a sampling frame requires identifying these intervention points. Larger costing studies, such as the Value TB study, have used a two-level sampling approach. The first level involved selecting countries based on criteria such as budget, study team capacity, data availability, representativeness, and feasibility. Countries with the highest TB burden, TB-HIV coinfection, and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) were prioritized. However, only one country with extensive MDR-TB hospitalization was included, and hospital costing was simplified due to limited study team capacity and time. The second level of sampling focused on selecting facilities within the chosen countries. Preliminary data were collected on TB interventions offered at different facility levels, population density, and TB notifications. The goal was to estimate unit costs for a comprehensive set of TB interventions and, where feasible, calculate nationally representative unit costs. Budget considerations influenced the selection of 24–30 facilities per country, following a standardized sampling strategy across the five countries. Regions were purposively sampled to reflect high, medium, and low TB burdens based on population size, TB cases, and urbanicity. A stratified random sampling approach ensured representation across strata such as level of care, ownership (public or private), and diagnostic interventions available (e.g., Xpert MTB/RIF, microscopy, or none). Facilities with very low TB service volumes were excluded. If a facility declined participation, a substitute facility from the same stratum was selected. The timeline for a costing study is typically around six months or longer. Costing selected TB services in a smaller sample (fewer than 10 sites) should take less than a year. However, costing all TB services in a nationally representative sample, as in the Value TB study, using current TB guidelines and the Value TB Costing Tool Suite, takes approximately one year. The average budget for one Value TB country, covering around 20 sites over 12 months, was approximately USD 100,000. This budget included travel, training, and meeting funds, as well as staff costs for principal investigators, study coordinators, data managers, and research assistants. Ethical approval is a critical component of costing studies, as they often involve reviewing medical records and interviewing staff. If the study is part of a larger existing study with ethical approval, expedited approval may be sought. For standalone TB costing studies, ethical approval must be obtained from all relevant parties, which can take one to six months depending on the setting and the inclusion of patient records or observations. This timeline must be factored into the overall study planning. Data collection design involves understanding the production process of TB services. This includes describing the outputs of interest and estimating costs per activity and output. Activities may occur at various platforms, such as health facilities, outreach programs, or household visits. Data collectors must reassess the production process of each TB service at a given facility, considering the delivery mechanism and setting. For example, interventions may be housed within the health system, at different facility types, in the community, or in facilities run by NGOs or faith-based organizations. At the facility level, TB interventions include vaccination, case detection and diagnosis, passive case finding (PCF), active case finding (ACF), intensified case finding (ICF), treatment, prevention, and infection control. Above the facility level, interventions include strategic planning, program reviews, national and regional meetings, surveys, management and information systems, supervision, procurement and supply chain management, specimen transportation, advocacy, technical assistance, training, accreditation, and quality assurance of laboratories, as well as community media and education campaigns. Data collectors must understand the workflow of the facility, including how services are provided, by whom, and the structure of service delivery. Discussions with clinic managers, TB nurses, or laboratory managers can provide valuable insights. Questions may address where patients are seen, whether space is shared between TB and other services, how TB and HIV care are integrated, where patients wait, which staff attend to patients, and how often patients come for treatment. Observing practices and mapping workflows can help identify inputs and resources that need to be measured. This process ensures that all aspects are costed and provides context for cost estimates within the facility. In laboratories, it is useful to speak with the laboratory manager and observe test processing. Standard operating procedures for diagnostic delivery can be verified through interviews with the laboratory manager. Workflow mapping helps identify inputs, such as capital and recurrent costs, which need to be measured. These inputs include building space, vehicles, equipment, training, and recurrent expenditures.
